content: CD155, also referred to as the poliovirus receptor, is a protein encoded by the PVR gene in humans. It is classified as a Type I transmembrane glycoprotein and belongs to the immunoglobulin superfamily. This protein is commonly known as the Poliovirus Receptor (PVR) due to its role in facilitating cellular infection by poliovirus in primates. However, its primary physiological function is to mediate the formation of intercellular adherens junctions between epithelial cells. The role of CD155 in the immune system remains incompletely understood, though it is hypothesized to contribute to intestinal humoral immune responses. Emerging evidence also suggests that CD155 may play a role in the positive selection of MHC-independent T cells within the thymus. The extracellular domain of CD155 facilitates cell attachment to the extracellular matrix protein vitronectin, while its intracellular domain interacts with the dynein light chain Tctex-1/DYNLT1. The PVR gene is specific to the primate lineage and serves as the cellular receptor for poliovirus during the initial step of viral replication. Structurally, CD155 is a transmembrane protein composed of three extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains, designated D1 through D3. The D1 domain is specifically recognized by the poliovirus. Low-resolution structural studies of CD155 in complex with poliovirus have been conducted using electron microscopy, while high-resolution structures of the ectodomains D1 and D2 have been elucidated through X-ray crystallography.
